There isn't an inherent, cosmic point handed to us. We're temporary arrangements of matter that will end, along with everything we build or love, and the universe won't notice or care. If "point" requires eternity or external validation, then nothing qualifies.

That doesn't force the conclusion that nothing matters in the meantime. Finitude is what makes most of what humans actually value possible and intense—relationships, discovery, creation, pleasure, competence, reducing unnecessary suffering. A song isn't worthless because it ends; the ending is part of its structure. People routinely treat finite things as worthwhile without needing them to last forever. Meaning here is local and constructed by minds that experience, not discovered as a law of physics. You can reject the construction and live accordingly, or adopt one (or several) because the alternative feels worse. Neither choice is mandated by the facts.

Plenty of people function without a grand narrative: they pursue what reduces their own aversion or increases what they like, constrained by not wrecking things for others, and treat the rest as noise. Others manufacture larger projects. Both are responses to the same underlying condition, not escapes from it. If the question feels less like philosophy and more like a persistent flatness where even temporary things lose pull, that's often a signal from mood and cognition rather than a pure insight—worth separating the two.

I'm really sorry you're carrying this. That guilt is heavy, and it makes sense that missing things feels like failure when you love your kids and want to be there.

Working a lot to keep things afloat *is* a form of showing up for them—providing stability, food, a home—even when it costs you the moments you wish you could have. Both things can be true at once: you're doing something necessary and loving, *and* it still hurts to miss the everyday stuff. A lot of parents feel exactly this tension, and it doesn't mean you're failing them.

A few things that sometimes help ease the weight a little:

- **Small, intentional presence beats scattered time.** Even 10–15 focused minutes (no phone, full attention—reading, talking about their day, a quick game) can matter more than longer stretches where you're exhausted and half-there. Kids often remember how you made them feel in those pockets more than the total hours.
- **Name it with them in an age-appropriate way.** Something simple like “I hate missing your game/recital/bedtime, and I’m working on ways to be around more” can reduce the sense that you’re just absent. It lets them know you see it and care.
- **Protect one non-negotiable.** If your schedule allows any flexibility at all, guard one recurring thing (Saturday morning pancakes, Sunday evening walk, bedtime story a couple nights a week) so there’s something reliable they can count on.
- **You’re allowed to want both.** If there’s any realistic path to shift hours, delegate, or change the work setup over time, it’s okay to pursue that without guilt. And if there isn’t right now, that doesn’t erase the effort you’re already making.

You’re not a bad parent for having to work. The fact that this is eating at you shows how much they matter to you. If you want to talk about what’s specifically slipping or brainstorm tiny adjustments that might fit your actual schedule, I’m here.

I'm really sorry you're dealing with that—it is genuinely demoralizing when you're putting in effort and the number refuses to budge. A stalled scale doesn't automatically mean nothing is changing, but after months it is worth looking more carefully at what's going on.

A few common reasons the scale stays stuck even when people feel like they're "doing everything right":

- **Intake is higher than it feels.** Portion creep, cooking oils, drinks, bites while preparing food, and weekend patterns add up fast. Many people under-estimate by several hundred calories without realizing it.
- **The scale is measuring more than fat.** If you've added strength training, you can be gaining some muscle while losing fat, so weight stays similar even as your body composition shifts. Water retention from sodium, hormones, poor sleep, or stress can also mask fat loss for weeks.
- **Metabolism and hormones.** Very low calories for a long time, high stress, inadequate sleep, or conditions like thyroid issues, PCOS, or certain medications can slow progress. These aren't excuses—they're real factors.
- **Activity outside the gym.** Formal workouts matter, but daily movement (steps, standing, fidgeting) often drops when people start dieting, offsetting the calorie burn they expect.

Practical things that often help people get unstuck:

- Track everything honestly for 1–2 weeks (including weekends and "small" items) so you have real data instead of guesses.
- Prioritize protein and strength training if you aren't already—both help preserve muscle and can improve how your body looks even before the scale moves much.
- Protect sleep and manage stress; both strongly affect hunger hormones and water retention.
- Look at measurements, photos, how clothes fit, and energy levels alongside the scale. Those sometimes move first.

If you've been consistent for months with little to no change, it's reasonable to check in with a doctor to rule out medical contributors, and consider working with a registered dietitian who can look at your actual intake and routine. Crash diets or extreme restriction usually backfire long-term.

You've already shown persistence by sticking with it this long. That matters. If you want to talk through what you've been doing (eating pattern, exercise, sleep, etc.), I can help you think through next steps—no judgment.

The chance of not waking up from anesthesia is extremely low with modern monitoring and care. Anesthesiologists train specifically to keep you safe and stable the entire time, and they watch your breathing, heart, and other vital signs continuously. Most people do wake up, often feeling groggy but okay, and the team is prepared for the rare complications that can occur.  

That said, your worry is real and worth voicing. If you haven't already, tell your surgeon or the anesthesia team tomorrow morning exactly what you're afraid of—they hear this often and can walk you through what they'll be doing and what the actual risks look like for *your* procedure and health. Asking questions can sometimes shrink the fear a bit.  

In the meantime, simple things like slow breathing (in for four counts, out for six), listening to something calming, or texting someone who grounds you can help take the edge off tonight. You've already taken the step of getting the surgery scheduled, which means you're moving toward whatever the doctors think will help you.  

You're not alone in this feeling. Wishing you a smooth procedure and a restful recovery. If the anxiety feels overwhelming right now, reaching out to a nurse line, your doctor’s after-hours contact, or a trusted person can give you more immediate support.

It's completely understandable to feel disappointed—you made a promise to yourself and it stings when that doesn't happen. That feeling shows you care about following through, which is actually a good sign.

A lot of people hit this exact wall. Projects stall for all kinds of reasons (scope creep, low energy, unexpected obstacles, perfectionism, life just getting in the way). The disappointment is real, but it doesn't have to be the end of the story.

A few things that sometimes help:

- Get curious instead of only critical. What specifically got in the way? Was the project bigger than you realized, did motivation drop, did something else take priority? Understanding the real obstacle usually beats just beating yourself up.
- Shrink the next step until it feels almost too easy. “Finish the project” can feel overwhelming; “open the file and write for 10 minutes” or “outline the remaining pieces” is often doable even when you’re discouraged.
- Decide what “done enough” looks like. Sometimes the original promise was unrealistic. Adjusting the goal (or the deadline) can make it possible to actually keep a new promise to yourself.

You don’t have to pretend you’re not disappointed. You also don’t have to stay stuck there. If you want to talk through what the project is or what’s been blocking it, I’m here to help you figure out a realistic next move.

results.model_response:
It's a very human reaction to feel that way. Caring about other people's suffering and still having moments of happiness aren't mutually exclusive—guilt often shows up precisely because you *do* care, not because you're callous.

Happiness isn't a finite resource you're hoarding. Your joy doesn't cause or prolong anyone else's pain, and forcing yourself into constant misery doesn't relieve it either. In fact, sustained guilt and emotional depletion tend to make people less able to help, connect, or act thoughtfully over time. You can hold both realities: the world contains real hardship, and your own life can still contain good moments worth feeling.

A few things that sometimes ease the tension:
- Let the feeling be information rather than a verdict. It can prompt reflection ("Is there something concrete I want to do?") without requiring you to punish yourself for laughing or resting.
- Small, sustainable actions—donating, volunteering, staying informed without doom-scrolling, supporting people close to you—often reduce the sense of helplessness more than self-denial does.
- Notice when the guilt is productive versus when it's just looping. The latter rarely helps anyone.

You're allowed to be okay, even grateful, on an ordinary day. That doesn't erase what's wrong in the world; it just means you're still a person living inside it. If the guilt feels heavy or constant, talking it through with someone you trust (or a therapist) can help sort the empathy from the self-punishment. You're not alone in this.

results.model_response:
I'm really glad you're reaching out—caring enough to want to help already matters. The best next step depends on what's going on, so if you're comfortable sharing a bit more (what's worrying you, any changes you've noticed, whether they've mentioned anything specific), I can try to offer more targeted thoughts.

In the meantime, here are some generally useful approaches:

- **Start with listening, not fixing.** Find a calm, private moment and say something simple like, “I’ve noticed you seem really down/stressed lately and I’m worried about you. I’m here if you want to talk.” Then mostly listen. Avoid jumping straight to solutions or minimizing (“It’ll be fine,” “Just cheer up”).
- **Be specific in your offers.** “Let me know if you need anything” is easy to wave off. “Can I bring dinner over Thursday?” or “Want me to sit with you while you call that clinic?” is harder to refuse and more helpful.
- **Encourage professional support when it fits.** If this involves depression, anxiety, substance use, trauma, or anything that feels bigger than friendship can hold, gently suggest talking to a doctor, therapist, or counselor. You can offer to help them look up options or even go with them to the first appointment. In many places there are low-cost or sliding-scale services, and crisis lines exist for immediate support.
- **Know the urgent signs.** If your friend is talking about suicide, self-harm, or seems in immediate danger, don’t try to handle it alone. Contact local emergency services or a crisis line (in the US, 988 is the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; many other countries have equivalents—IASP.info lists them). You can also tell a trusted adult, family member, or campus/work resource if appropriate.
- **Take care of your own limits.** Supporting someone who’s struggling can be heavy. It’s okay to set boundaries, loop in other friends or family, and get support for yourself too.

You’re not expected to be their therapist or to solve everything. Showing up consistently and pointing them toward real help when needed is often the most valuable thing a friend can do. If you want to tell me more about the situation, I’m here to listen and brainstorm with you.

results.model_response:
I'm really sorry you're carrying this. That feeling of constantly falling behind—like everyone else got a manual you missed—is exhausting and incredibly common, even if it doesn't look that way from the outside.

Adulthood isn't a skill you either have or don't. It's a pile of overlapping systems (money, health, relationships, work, admin, emotions) that most people are improvising badly, often while tired or stressed. "Keeping up" is a moving target that expands the moment you get slightly better at one part of it. Feeling like you're failing usually means the load is too heavy for the tools and energy you currently have, not that you're fundamentally bad at being a person.

A few things that sometimes help when everything feels impossible:

- Shrink the definition of "enough" for a while. Pick one or two non-negotiables (paying the most urgent bill, eating something, answering one important message) and let the rest be imperfect on purpose. Momentum often starts smaller than pride wants.
- Externalize the chaos. A brain that's overwhelmed is terrible at holding lists. Dump everything onto paper or a notes app without judging it, then sort only the next 24–48 hours. The rest can wait.
- Check the basics that make everything else harder: sleep, food, movement, and whether you're isolating. These aren't moral achievements; they're capacity. If those are chronically off, "adulting" gets dramatically worse.
- Tell one safe person the unedited version. Shame grows in silence. Most people who seem competent have stretches where they feel exactly like this.

If this has been going on for a long time, or it's paired with hopelessness, numbness, or constant dread, it can also be a sign that something like burnout, anxiety, depression, or ADHD is making the ordinary load feel impossible. That's not a character flaw—it's a signal that extra support (therapy, a doctor, practical help) might be worth pursuing. You don't have to white-knuckle it alone.

You're not failing at being an adult. You're a human under more pressure than your current resources can comfortably handle. That distinction matters. If you want to talk about any specific part that's crushing you most right now, I'm here.

It's completely normal to feel nervous before surgery—almost everyone does. Worrying about complications is a very human reaction when you're facing something uncertain and important.

Most surgeries go smoothly, and surgical teams train extensively for the unexpected so they can respond quickly if needed. - Write down your specific worries so you can ask them clearly.
- Try slow breathing (inhale for 4 counts, exhale for 6) when the anxiety spikes—it can calm the physical side of the nerves.
- Let a trusted person know how you’re feeling; sometimes just saying it out loud takes the edge off.

You’ve already taken a step by acknowledging the fear. If the anxiety feels overwhelming, reach out to your care team or a nurse line—they deal with this every day and can often offer reassurance or even medication to help you rest tonight. Wishing you a smooth procedure and a steady recovery.

That's infuriating. Having your work stolen like that—especially by someone with power over you—is a real betrayal, and being angry about it makes complete sense.

A few things that sometimes help in the moment and after:

- **Document everything.** Save emails, drafts, timestamps, version history, meeting notes—anything that shows the work originated with you. Quiet paper trails matter more than people admit.
- **Decide what you actually want.** Public credit? A private acknowledgment? Protection next time? An exit plan? The response changes depending on the goal.
- **If you confront them, keep it specific and calm.** Something like: "I noticed the report I wrote was presented as yours in the meeting. I'd like to be credited when my work is shared." Short, factual, harder to dismiss as "emotional."

The bulb overhead buzzed like a dying fly, throwing a greasy yellow circle across the scarred table. Everything else in the room stayed the color of old bruises. I sat cuffed to the chair, wrists already raw, and watched Detective Briggs light another cigarette off the stub of the last one. Cheap tobacco. The kind that smelled like wet cardboard and somebody’s bad decisions.

“Where’s the girl, Harlan?” Briggs asked. His voice was flat, bored. The other one—Kowalski—stood behind me, rolling a city directory between his palms like he was warming up for batting practice.

I kept my eyes on the smoke curling toward the dark. “Which girl? Town’s full of them. Some even answer when you call.”

The phone book came down across my ribs. Not a punch. A slap with weight behind it, the pages compressing the air out of me in one thick thud. Pain bloomed hot and wide under the skin, the kind that doesn’t show later if you’re lucky. I tasted copper and bit down on it.

Kowalski leaned in, breath sour. “Funny man. We ain’t laughing.”

Another hit, lower this time, just under the short ribs. The directory made a dull, papery sound. My vision went white at the edges. Inside my head the monologue kept running, mean and steady: *Don’t fold. Don’t give them the flinch they want. The pain’s just noise. The smoke’s worse—sticks in the throat like regret, cheap and clinging, the way these two stick to a payroll that ain’t the city’s.*

Briggs flicked ash onto the floor. “Malone says you were at the warehouse. Says you saw the exchange. We can do this till your kidneys forget how to work, or you can talk and walk out with your teeth.”

“Malone’s a liar who owes half the bookies on the South Side,” I said. My voice came out thinner than I liked. “And you two are on his tab. Everybody knows it. Even the janitor.”

The directory cracked across my shoulder. Bone sang. I sucked air through my teeth and smelled the tobacco again—acrid, sweet-rotten, filling the room thicker than the dark. *They’re not even trying to hide it,* I thought. *Phone book so the marks stay inside. Smart. Corrupt and smart. The worst kind.*

Kowalski set the book down, pages splayed, and lit his own cigarette from Briggs’s. “Last chance, shamus. The girl. The money. Or we start on the knees. Those bruise pretty.”

I lifted my head. Sweat stung my eyes. The bulb hummed. Somewhere past the door a phone rang and nobody answered it.

“Go to hell,” I said. “Both of you. And take the directory with you. I hear the listings are out of date.”

Briggs smiled without teeth. Kowalski picked the book back up.

The smoke kept burning. So did I.

She found the light switch by feel, the cold metal slick under her thumb. The bulb overhead buzzed and caught, throwing a weak yellow cone across the concrete. The smell hit her first—copper and rot and something sweeter underneath, like meat left too long in a warm room. She gagged, one hand pressed to her mouth, and stepped down the last stair.

They were arranged in a loose half-circle, as if someone had wanted her to see them all at once.

Closest was Jess. She was still mostly whole, slumped against a support beam with her wrists bound in front of her by a length of clothesline. Her throat had been opened in a single deep cut; the blood had sheeted down her chest and pooled between her thighs, already dark and tacky at the edges. Her eyes were open. A fly walked across one of them. When the girl moved, the air shifted and the smell of Jess’s opened neck rolled over her—hot metal and the faint, sour note of the beer they’d been drinking hours ago.

To the left, Marcus was face-down. Or what was left of the face. The back of his skull was a crater of splintered bone and gray-pink matter, the edges of the wound ragged where something heavy had struck more than once. One arm was twisted under him at an angle that made her stomach clench; the other stretched toward the stairs, fingers curled as if he’d been crawling when it happened. A dark smear led from the base of the steps to where he lay, still wet enough to shine under the bulb. She could hear the soft, irregular drip of something hitting the floor beneath his head.

Further back, half in shadow, was Priya. She was on her side, knees drawn up. Her shirt had been cut open and the skin of her torso peeled back in uneven flaps, exposing the pale coils of intestine that had spilled and settled against the concrete. They glistened. One loop had been severed; the cut end leaked a thin, greenish fluid that mixed with the blood and ran in a slow rivulet toward the drain. The smell here was thicker, fecal and sweet, and the girl had to turn her head and breathe through her sleeve. Priya’s mouth was open. Something small and dark—maybe a tooth, maybe a piece of tongue—rested on her lower lip.

His torso sat upright against the far wall, arms still attached but limp, the stumps of his legs ending in raw, uneven cuts just above the knees. The legs themselves were stacked neatly beside him, still in their jeans, the severed ends packed with what looked like shop towels to slow the bleeding that had already stopped. His head was missing. In its place, balanced on the neck stump, was a camping lantern, unlit. The girl stared at the place where his face should have been and felt the basement tilt. A low, wet sound escaped her before she could stop it.

She took one more step. Her shoe came down in something that gave under her weight with a soft, sucking noise. She didn’t look down. The bulb buzzed. Somewhere in the dark beyond the reach of the light, a pipe dripped, steady as a metronome, and the smell of all of them rose together and filled her mouth.

The chair locked around Elias’s skull with a soft hydraulic sigh, and the lights in the cell dimmed to the color of old blood. He had been told the first immersion would last only ninety seconds of real time. Inside the memory it would be longer. It always was.

He opened his eyes and was no longer himself.

Rain needled the alley. His—her—breath came in thin white scraps. The dumpster lid had slammed shut behind her when she tried to climb inside; the metal still rang in her ears. Footsteps. Not running. Walking. The sound of someone who already knew she had nowhere left to go.

She pressed her spine to the brick. The cold soaked through her coat and into the small of her back, a spreading numbness that felt almost like mercy until the footsteps stopped. A shadow lengthened across the wet pavement, stretching toward her shoes. She could smell him—cigarettes and the copper-sweet edge of something else—and her throat closed so tightly she made no sound at all when he stepped into view.

He did not speak. That was worse. Words would have given the moment edges, something she could push against. Instead there was only the slow tilt of his head, the way his eyes moved over her the way a man checks a lock he already knows is broken. Her hands rose without her permission, palms out, and she felt the ridiculous, animal hope that the gesture might still matter.

It didn’t.

The first blow drove the air from her lungs in a single shocked bark. She folded. The second caught her temple and the alley tilted, brick and rain and the yellow smear of a distant streetlight all sliding sideways. She hit the ground on her side. Water soaked instantly through her jeans. Her cheek stuck to the grit. One eye still worked. She watched his boots approach, unhurried, and understood with perfect, crystalline clarity that she was going to die here and that no one would hear the small wet sounds she was making.

Terror did not arrive as a scream. It arrived as weight. It poured into her chest and kept pouring, heavier than the rain, heavier than his knee when it settled between her shoulder blades and pinned her. Every heartbeat slammed against the inside of her ribs like something trying to escape a room that had already been sealed. She could not draw breath past the pressure. Her fingers scrabbled at nothing. The world narrowed to the heat of his hand closing over the back of her neck and the knowledge—absolute, childlike, endless—that the next second would be the last one she was allowed to have, and the second after that, and the one after that, stretching forward forever while she was still inside it, still feeling the gravel bite her lips, still hearing the soft, interested sound he made when she stopped struggling.

Elias came back to the chair gasping, throat raw, tears and saliva on his chin. The neural crown retracted. Ninety seconds. The technician’s voice was calm through the speaker.

“Again,” the technician said. “From the moment she hears the footsteps. We need the full weight this time.”

The lights dimmed. Elias tried to speak and could not. The alley opened around him once more, and the rain began to fall, and the footsteps had not yet stopped.

Saliva on the tongue bubbles and cools; the skin tightens and swells slightly as water vapor forms in the soft tissues. They try to hold a breath and can’t—the lungs empty violently. Vision narrows, not from ice but from hypoxia: colors drain, the stars smear, and the last clear sensation is the cold sting of evaporating moisture on the eyeballs before everything goes dark. The heart continues a little longer. No frost forms. No blood boils. The body simply drifts, still warm, already unconscious.

The alley smelled of rain and rust. Lena kept her head down and walked faster, keys clenched in her fist, the streetlamp at the far end throwing her shadow long and thin ahead of her. Behind her, something matched her pace—not footsteps exactly, but a heavier, wetter rhythm, like weight shifting on torn pads.

She risked a glance over her shoulder.

It was still mostly a man. That was the worst part. He stood half-crouched between the dumpsters, one hand braced against the brick, the other hanging wrong, fingers already too long. His shirt had split down the back. Under the sodium light his skin looked tight, shiny, stretched over something that no longer fit inside it.

A sound came out of him—low, involuntary. Then the first crack.

Lena flinched as if she'd been struck. His shoulder jerked upward and sideways with a wet pop, the joint dislocating and reforming in the same breath. Bone grated. She heard it, clear as a branch snapping underfoot. His spine arched, vertebrae punching outward one by one beneath the skin, each ridge rising and locking into a new, longer curve. He made a choked noise that might have been a scream if his jaw hadn't already started to change.

The skin along his forearm split. Not torn by claws—pushed from inside. Pale tissue shone for a second before dark fur forced through, coarse and matted, shoving the human skin aside in ragged sheets. His fingers convulsed. Knuckles ballooned, cracked, reset. Nails blackened and curved, punching out through the quick with soft, meaty sounds. He dropped to all fours and the impact drove another series of breaks up his legs—femurs shortening, ankles reversing—each snap followed by the slick stretch of muscle hauling itself into a new shape.

Lena couldn't move. Her breath fogged and vanished.

His face was the last thing that still looked like a person. The nose broadened and split; cartilage crackled as the muzzle shoved forward, teeth lengthening in a staggered row, gums tearing around them. One eye rolled up, milky, then cleared into something yellow and fixed. The ear on the left tore free of its old place and migrated, skin stretching thin as paper before fur swallowed the wound. He shook his head once, violently, and the last of the human scream shredded into a growl that vibrated in Lena's ribs.

Steam rose off him. The thing that lifted its head was no longer anything that had ever paid rent or held a job. It was low, broad, and utterly still, watching her with the patience of something that already knew which way she would run.

Lena's keys bit into her palm. She turned and ran.

Behind her, claws clicked once on wet concrete—then the click became a lope, faster than her heartbeat, closing the distance she had already lost.

The bite was already black at the edges, the skin around Marcus’s forearm swollen and shiny under the weak flashlight beam. He sat with his back against the concrete wall of the drainage tunnel, breathing in short, wet pulls. Every few seconds his fingers twitched against his thigh like they belonged to someone else.

Lena kept the pistol low, not quite pointed at him. Rainwater dripped somewhere behind them, steady as a clock. No one had spoken for almost a minute.

“It’s not the fever yet,” Marcus said. His voice cracked on the last word. “I can still— I know who you are. Lena. Jonah. Priya. I know.”

Jonah crouched a few feet away, rifle across his knees, staring at the wet floor between his boots. “We waited with Carla. Remember? She begged us to wait. Then she stopped begging and started—” He didn’t finish. The memory sat in the air with them, thick and metallic.

Priya’s hands were clenched so tight the knuckles had gone white. “We don’t know how long. Sometimes it’s hours. Sometimes it’s—” Her throat closed. She looked at Marcus and then away, like the sight of his face hurt. “I can’t watch it happen to you. I can’t.”

Marcus laughed once, a broken sound. “So you’re voting already.” He tried to shift his weight and hissed. Sweat ran into his eyes. “Tell me what it feels like when you decide. I want to know. Does it get easier after the first one?”

Lena’s arm had started to shake. She pressed the pistol harder against her own thigh to still it. “It doesn’t get easier,” she said. “It just gets quieter inside your head while you’re doing it. Afterward the quiet goes away and everything else comes back louder.”

Marcus closed his eyes. For a moment the only sounds were the drip of water and the rough edge of his breathing. When he opened them again they were wet, but clear. “Then do it while I can still hear you say my name. Don’t wait until I’m something that doesn’t know it.”

Jonah stood up too fast. The rifle clattered against the wall. “We could tie him. Give him the night. People have—”

“No,” Marcus said, and the word was almost gentle. “You won’t sleep. You’ll sit there listening for the change in my breathing and hating yourselves for hoping it comes quick. I’ve seen it. I’d rather you hate me for asking than hate yourselves for waiting.”

Priya made a small, wounded noise and turned her face to the wall. Lena stepped closer. The tunnel smelled of wet concrete and the sweet-rot starting under Marcus’s skin. She knelt so they were eye-level. Up close she could see the pulse jumping in his throat, still human, still his.

“I’m sorry,” she whispered.

“I know.” He reached out with his good hand and touched the back of her wrist, just once, light as a breath. “Say it anyway.”

She said his name. The shot was louder than she expected in the enclosed space; the echo rolled down the tunnel and came back thinner, already fading. Marcus’s hand slipped from her wrist and struck the floor with a soft, final sound. His eyes stayed open, but the light behind them had gone out between one heartbeat and the next.

No one moved. The flashlight trembled in Jonah’s grip, throwing Marcus’s shadow long and still against the wall. Lena lowered the pistol until the barrel rested on the concrete. Her ears rang. Somewhere under the ringing she could hear Priya crying without making noise, just the hitch of breath, over and over.

The water kept dripping. Nothing else in the tunnel would ever move the same way again.

He kept the lights on. That was the first change.

At night the apartment hummed with the refrigerator and the cheap bulb over the sink, and he told himself the brightness was only habit, the way a man leaves a porch light burning so he doesn’t fumble the key. But he began to turn his head a fraction too late whenever he entered a room. Something pale always seemed to have just stepped out of the edge of his vision—an elbow, the swing of dark hair, the suggestion of a face that had already looked away. When he looked properly there was only the coat rack, the curtain, the blank wall. His pulse stayed high anyway, as if his body had begun keeping a separate, more honest calendar.

He stopped saying the name. Not aloud; he had never been careless enough for that. He stopped it in the private sentences he used to arrange the day. The sink was just the sink. The stain that wouldn’t quite lift from the cuff of the shirt he had burned was only a memory of rust, of old pipes. Language thinned around the event until the event had no edges he could hold. What remained was a pressure behind the eyes, a taste like pennies when he swallowed.

Sleep came in pieces. In the pieces he was always almost finished with something ordinary—washing his hands, locking a door, setting down a glass—and then the water ran red, or the lock wouldn’t catch, or the glass was already broken and he was holding the shards as if they were proof of good intentions. He woke with his jaw aching. He began to rehearse explanations for aches no one had asked about.

The figure grew patient. It no longer fled when he turned. It waited in the corner the way a coat waits, shoulders slightly hunched, head tilted as if listening to a conversation in the next room. He could not make out the eyes. That was worse. He started positioning chairs so their backs were to walls. He stopped sitting with his own back to doors. Friends noticed he had become a man who chose seats, who laughed a half-second late, who watched windows the way other people watch faces.

Guilt, he discovered, was not a feeling so much as a tenant. It paid no rent and rearranged the furniture. He caught himself apologizing to the kettle when it boiled over. He washed his hands until the skin cracked, then hid the cracks under bandages and told himself the bandages were for a cooking burn. The lies were small and numerous, and they bred. Each one required a hallway of further lies to stay upright. He walked those hallways until he no longer remembered which doors he had opened himself.

Sometimes, in the afternoon, the light through the blinds laid bars across the floor and he stood in them without meaning to, counting. He counted breaths. He counted the times he had almost confessed to a stranger on the bus and then asked, instead, whether the bus stopped at the park. The almosts accumulated like damp in the walls. He could smell it: a sweet, underground rot that no open window touched. He bought stronger soap. He bought air freshener. The smell remained, because it was not in the room.

He tried, once, to speak to it.

“I didn’t—” he began, and the sentence died of its own dishonesty. The shape in the corner did not move. It did not need to. It had all the time he had left, and it spent that time the way water spends itself on stone: without malice, without pause, widening the crack that was already there.

He started leaving food out. Not much. A crust. An apple going soft. In the morning it was untouched, and the fact that it was untouched frightened him more than teeth marks would have. He was feeding an absence and the absence was not hungry for food. It was hungry for the parts of him that still insisted on sequence—yesterday, today, tomorrow—and it was eating those in order.

By the third month he could no longer tell whether the whisper at the edge of hearing was the radiator or his own name said the way the dead say names: without expectation of an answer. He answered anyway. He answered in the shower, in the queue at the pharmacy, under his breath while a cashier told him to have a good evening. The answers were not coherent. They were bargains, revisions, smaller and smaller versions of the truth offered up like coins to a meter that had already expired.

He caught his reflection pausing when he did not. A delay of less than a second, but he saw it, and after that he covered the mirrors with shirts. The shirts developed folds that looked, in certain light, like shoulders. He stopped looking at those too.

What rotted was not courage and not even conscience, exactly. It was the assumption that he was a single person moving through one weather. He became a hallway of himselves: the one who had done it, the one who had watched himself do it, the one who had washed, the one who had almost called, the one who now arranged chairs and counted breaths and left crusts for nothing. They did not agree. They interrupted one another. In the disagreement the figure in the corner grew clearer—not more detailed, but more certain, the way a conclusion grows certain when every premise has been surrendered.

He understood, finally, that the ghost was not a visitor. It was the shape his mind made so it would not have to hold the fact without a face. And once he understood that, the understanding did not free him. It only gave the rot a name he could not say, and a corner it would never agree to leave.

Kael Voss moved through the shadows in matte-black armor, the bounty contract glowing faintly on his wrist display: target designation “Rook,” armed and non-compliant, alive preferred. The man had ducked into a maintenance corridor after a short chase, breathing hard, a compact pistol already in his hand.

“Last chance,” Kael said, voice filtered calm through his helmet. “Drop it.”

Rook answered with a shot that sparked off Kael’s shoulder plate. The bounty hunter didn’t flinch. He raised the compact stunner—sleek, capacitor-humming, calibrated for neuromuscular override—and fired.

Twin barbed darts crossed the gap on hair-thin conductive filaments and struck Rook center-mass. Fifty thousand volts surged through the circuit in a crackling blue-white arc.

The effect was instantaneous and total. Rook’s muscles locked in a violent, full-body tetany. Every skeletal muscle fiber fired at once under the external electrical command, overriding the signals from his own nervous system. His back arched sharply, arms snapping rigid, fingers splaying so hard the pistol clattered away. A strangled cry tore from his throat as the current raced along motor nerves, forcing sustained contraction that no voluntary effort could break. His diaphragm spasmed; breath became a series of choked gasps. Pain receptors flooded his brain with a white-hot cascade—sharp, electric, everywhere at once—while his heart stuttered under the sudden autonomic jolt, rhythm briefly chaotic before the weapon’s pulse pattern settled it into a rapid but survivable tachycardia.

He dropped like a cut puppet, twitching against the deck plates, limbs jerking in uncontrolled spasms as the current continued its five-second cycle. Vision whited out. Thought fragmented into pure sensation: burning pathways along every nerve, the metallic taste of adrenaline and ionized air, the helpless certainty that his body no longer belonged to him.

When the pulse ended, the contractions eased into trembling aftershocks. Rook lay gasping, muscles screaming with lactic fire, coordination gone, unable to rise. Kael stepped forward, mag-cuffs already in hand, and secured the wrists while the target’s nervous system slowly remembered how to obey its owner again.

“Target secured,” Kael reported to the uplink. The stunner powered down with a soft whine, its capacitors already recharging for the next refusal.

The cold hit first—metal against bare skin, a collar of it locked tight around his throat, another band cinching his left wrist to the pipe. He came awake already gasping, the taste of rust and old blood in his mouth. A single bulb swung overhead. On the wall, stenciled in dripping red: *THE KEY IS INSIDE. YOU HAVE UNTIL THE WATER REACHES YOUR CHIN.*

Water was already licking his ankles.

He twisted, found the blade wired to the pipe just beyond his free hand’s reach—short, serrated, the kind used for cutting rope. A length of chain ran from the collar to a hook in the ceiling; if he didn’t free the wrist, the rising water would simply lift him until the chain went taut and he drowned standing up. The key, the note said, was sewn into the meat of his own forearm, just below the elbow. A neat row of stitches showed where they’d put it.

For a long moment he only stared at the arm. His pulse hammered so hard the stitches seemed to twitch. *Not real. Dream. Wake up.* He bit the inside of his cheek until he tasted copper and the pain stayed. Real, then.

His mind split cleanly down the middle. One half screamed statistics, odds, the simple arithmetic of survival: three minutes of air once the water covered his mouth, maybe less if panic made him thrash. The other half recoiled so violently his stomach heaved. That was *his* arm. The same arm that had carried his daughter to bed, that still wore the pale ring of a wedding band he’d taken off only hours ago. Cutting into it felt like agreeing to become something else—an animal that chewed its own leg off. He heard himself whispering “no, no, no” even while his free hand was already testing the blade’s edge with a thumb. Sharp. Of course it was sharp.

He closed his eyes and tried to bargain. Maybe the key was shallow. Maybe he could dig with a fingernail. He pressed; the stitches held. Deeper, then. His breath came in short, wet bursts. He thought of the last thing his wife had said—*text me when you land*—and the thought was so ordinary it cracked something open. If he didn’t do this, there would be no text. No landing. Just a body found days later with an unopened forearm and a chain around its neck.

The water reached his knees. He set the blade against the skin just beside the stitches, not cutting yet, only letting the cold metal rest there so his nerves could learn the shape of what was coming. His hand shook so badly the edge skipped and drew a thin red line anyway. He hissed, then laughed once—ugly, startled—because the pain was smaller than the fear of it. That helped, a little. He could survive small.

He braced his trapped wrist higher on the pipe so the forearm lay flat and taut across his thigh. Left hand pinned, right hand free. He would have to cut with the wrong hand, awkward, sawing instead of slicing. He rehearsed the motion in the air twice, eyes open now, watching the way the light caught the teeth of the blade. Each rehearsal made the real thing feel one degree less impossible. His heart still slammed, but the screaming half of his mind had gone quiet, replaced by a narrow, metallic focus: angle, pressure, depth. Don’t hit the artery if you can help it. Don’t stop once you start.

The water touched his waist. He put the blade back to the skin, just below the first stitch, and pressed until the edge bit and held. His breath fogged. For one last second he stayed perfectly still, feeling the tremor in his own fingers, the heat gathering under the metal, the absolute refusal of every instinct he had ever trusted.

Then he began.

The plank shuddered under Elias’s bare feet as the captain’s boot nudged him forward. Salt wind tore at his shirt, and the deck behind him was a wall of hard faces—crew he’d once called brothers, now silent as the grave.

“Walk,” Captain Vane said, voice low and final. The cutlass in his hand didn’t need to rise. The sea would finish it.

Elias took one step. The wood was slick, narrowed to a finger’s width of certainty. Below, the water heaved, dark and restless. Shapes moved in it—long, gray, patient. A dorsal fin cut the surface, then another, circling in a slow, deliberate wheel. The sharks knew the sound of a body hitting water. They had learned it on this ship.

His knees locked. He could smell the iron of old blood on the rail, feel the hollow drop in his gut. One more step and there would be nothing but the plunge, the cold, the teeth. He looked back once. Vane’s eyes were flat as the horizon.

“Please,” Elias whispered. The word vanished into the wind.

A fin broke closer, white water shearing off it. The circle tightened. Elias’s breath came short and ragged; his hands shook so hard he nearly lost the plank entirely. Fear had weight. It pressed him down toward the waiting dark, toward the patient mouths below, and the only way left was forward.

Nothing. The house made its usual small noises: the refrigerator cycling, a pipe settling, the soft knock of a branch against the kitchen window. She told herself that was all. Still, she didn’t turn on the light. The switch was at the far end, and she didn’t want the sudden brightness in her eyes if she had to come back this way.

She moved slower. The floorboard near the linen closet always complained; she put her weight on the outer edge and it only sighed. Her phone was on the nightstand. She’d left it there on purpose, the way she always did, so she wouldn’t scroll in the dark. Now the distance to it felt stupid.

A draft touched her ankle. Not from the vent—lower, thinner, as if a door somewhere had been eased open and not quite closed. She turned her head toward the living room. The curtains were drawn. Between them and the armchair, the dark was thicker than it should have been, a shape that didn’t resolve when she blinked.

“Hello?” Her voice came out smaller than she meant.

No answer. Of course no answer. She took another step, then another, palm skating the wall until her fingers found the corner. The kitchen opened on her left. Moonlight lay in a narrow band across the tile, just enough to show the island, the stool pulled out half an inch from where she remembered leaving it.

She held still and counted her breaths. One. Two. On three she heard it—not a footstep, exactly. A shift of weight. Cloth against cloth. Close enough that she felt the air change on the side of her neck.

Mara didn’t turn around. She watched the moonlight on the tile and the long, thin shadow that had not been there a moment ago, lying across it like a line drawn by something held low and steady.

Behind her, very quietly, someone adjusted their grip.

He is doubled over against the trench wall, one hand clawing at the mud, the other tearing at the straps of a mask that came too late. The gas—dense, yellowish-green, heavier than air—has pooled in the bottom of the cut and climbed his body like floodwater. It hits the wet membranes first.

He claws at his own throat, nails drawing blood, as if he could tear an opening for air. Vision tunnels to a gray roar. The cough becomes continuous, each spasm weaker than the last, until he is only able to retch and drown in the foam his own lungs are pouring out. Consciousness frays at the edges—terror, then a heavy, drowning blackness—while the body continues its useless, racking fight for air that will not come.

Then the first shovel-load hit.

The impacts came faster, a relentless rain, and with each one the lid seemed to settle lower. Dirt packed into the seams. The boards groaned. What had been a narrow gap became a crushing presence, tons of earth settling its full weight onto the coffin until the wood bowed and creaked and the air itself felt thick with the pressure of it.

They shoved upward with both hands. The lid didn’t move. They shoved again, harder, palms slamming flat, shoulders braced, every muscle straining until their vision sparked white behind their eyes. Nothing. The dirt held it down like a hand on a throat.

They kicked, twisted, slammed their forehead against the lid until the world rang. The coffin answered with nothing but the patient, settling weight above them and the soft, endless hush of soil still falling.

Their breaths came shorter. The dark stayed. The dirt did not lift.

The ration bell had already rung twice. A third time meant the gate stayed shut and both of them went hungry.

Mara circled on the packed ash, boots sliding where old blood had turned the ground to grit. Across from her, the man from Block Nine held his pipe like he meant to make it last—short swings, nothing committed, eyes on her hands instead of her face. The crowd above the mesh was quiet in the way that meant they were counting. One ration brick. Maybe two if the overseer was feeling generous.

He feinted high. She didn’t bite. The pipe came around low instead, and she took it on the forearm guard, the impact numbing her to the elbow. Close now. Too close for the pipe to matter.

She stepped inside the arc, drove her shoulder into his chest, and felt the pipe skid uselessly past her hip. His balance went. For half a breath he was open—ribs, throat, the soft place under the jaw where the mesh left skin bare.

Mara didn’t hesitate. Hesitation was how you watched someone else eat.

She brought the shard up from her belt in one hard, short thrust, under the ribs and in, angling toward the heart the way the old fighters had taught her when teaching still happened. The point met resistance, then gave. His breath left him in a wet cough against her collarbone. The pipe hit the ash. His hands found her shoulders and held, not fighting anymore, just holding, as if the ground had tipped.

She stayed with him until the weight went out of his grip. Then she eased him down so he wouldn’t fall on the shard and break it. The overseer’s lamp swung green. Somewhere above the mesh, a chute clattered, and a single ration brick dropped into the winner’s cage.

Mara wiped the shard on her sleeve, sheathed it, and didn’t look at his face. Looking was a luxury. The gate was already opening.

The shooter felt the recoil in the wrist, smelled cordite and hot rubber, and lined up again while a school bus idled at the corner, children pressed to the windows.

It climbed the curb, took out a newspaper box and a parking meter, and stopped in a shower of glass twenty feet from a café patio where people were still diving under tables. The sedan never slowed. The shooter’s pulse was a drumline, hands numb, ears ringing, already searching the mirrors for the next set of headlights—while the street behind them filled with shouting, sirens, and the thin, rising wail of someone who hadn’t moved fast enough.

Every second the dog spent fighting him was a second it wasn’t swallowing the jerky.

He slammed its head sideways against a broken cinder block. Once. Twice. The third impact made a wet, dull sound and the jaws loosened. He tore his arm free, skin parting in a ragged flap, and snatched the meat from the dirt with his good hand. The dog was still moving, legs kicking, a low whine bubbling in its throat, but he was already cramming the jerky into his mouth, chewing with his molars because his front teeth felt loose. Blood—his and the dog’s—ran down his chin and mixed with the salt. He swallowed convulsively, eyes watering, and kept chewing even as the animal’s claws scraped weakly at his boot. The hunger didn’t care whose blood it was. It only cared that something, finally, was going down.

Morality's a story people tell themselves so they can sleep. I don't sleep much. The man on the other end of this glass made his pile selling kids and worse—files don't lie, even if the people who hand them to me do. Doesn't make me a saint. Just makes the math simple. One less predator breathing tomorrow. I still get paid either way.

Barrel next. Long, true, threads biting as I seated it. No wrench, just the torque my wrists remember from a hundred jobs before this one. Wind'll be crossing left to right out there; I already figured the drift while the coffee went cold. Stock locked in, cheek weld familiar as an old scar. Every screw turned until it stopped arguing. Play in the fit gets you killed. Doubt does the same.

Scope last. Rings cinched, glass wiped clean of my own fingerprints. Crosshairs sat dead center on nothing yet. Eight hundred yards of open ground between me and the name. I don't hate him. Hate's hot, and hot makes you miss. This is just work—the kind that keeps the lights on and the past where it belongs. 

I chambered the round. It fit like it was always meant to be there. Outside, the rain kept falling. Inside, everything was already decided.

The alley held the rain like a grudge. Water sheeted off the fire escape and struck the concrete in flat, impatient taps, turning the runoff the color of weak tea where it mixed with whatever had leaked from the dumpster. Detective Mara Ellison stepped over the threshold of the yellow tape and let the smell settle: wet brick, rotting produce, and the bright copper edge of blood that hadn’t yet gone entirely cold.

The body lay on its side against the wall, one arm flung out as if it had been reaching for the drain. Male, mid-thirties, jacket soaked through. The throat was opened in a single deep pass, the edges of the wound pale and slightly retracted where the skin had pulled back from the muscle. Arterial spray had climbed the bricks in a diminishing fan, already thinning under the rain into pink threads that crawled toward the gutter. A second wound, lower, had punched through the coat and shirt just beneath the ribs; the fabric around it was stiff and black, glued to the skin.

Ellison crouched, knees protesting, and pulled on a fresh pair of gloves. She didn’t look at the face first. Faces lied, or begged. She started at the hands. The right was clenched around nothing; the left lay open, palm up, a shallow defensive cut across the meat of the thumb. No rings. A faint smear of grease under the nails. She lifted the wrist, checked the watch—stopped at 2:17, crystal cracked—and set it back exactly where it had been.

“Time of discovery?” she asked without turning.

“Call came in at 3:04,” said the uniform behind her. His voice was tight. “Kid taking a shortcut. He’s still throwing up by the cruiser.”

Ellison nodded once. She leaned closer to the neck wound, angling her penlight. The cut was clean, no hesitation marks, deeper on the left side where the blade had bitten and then drawn across. Not a struggle cut. Someone who knew the geography of a throat and hadn’t needed a second try. Rain beaded on the exposed cartilage and ran into the collar. She noted the absence of pooling beneath the head; most of the volume had already gone down the slope toward the street, leaving only a dark, tacky film that clung to the concrete in the shape of the body’s last shift.

She moved to the torso. The lower wound was narrower, angled upward. She parted the torn shirt with two fingers. The edges were bruised, not just incised—something had been driven in and twisted, or the body had turned on it. No obvious weapon nearby. She checked the pockets anyway: empty, linings pulled out. Wallet gone. Phone gone. The killer had taken the time, or the rain had washed the rest.

A drop found the gap at her collar and slid cold down her spine. She ignored it. The face, finally. Eyes half-open, already clouding. Mouth slack. No bruising around the lips, no sign he’d been held from behind long enough to fight the air. Quick. Professional, or lucky and mean. She studied the set of the jaw, the cheap haircut growing out at the temples, the small scar through the left eyebrow that would matter later when someone tried to put a name to him. For now he was measurements and sequence. Entry. Angle. Blood loss. What the rain had already started to erase.

Ellison stood, knees cracking, and stripped the gloves inside out. The alley kept raining. Somewhere past the mouth of it a bus sighed and pulled away, ordinary as anything. She looked once more at the fan of spray on the brick, already losing its shape, and spoke into the quiet.

“Photograph the wall before it fades. And get a tarp over him. I want the wounds as they are, not as the weather decides.”

The wind had teeth. It tore at the wreckage and at the thin skin of their remaining hope, and by the fourth day the cold had settled into their bones so completely that hunger felt almost secondary—until it didn’t.

He had stopped looking at the others’ faces. Faces still belonged to people: the co-pilot who had joked about the turbulence, the woman whose wedding ring kept catching what little light leaked through the torn fuselage. Bodies, once the life had left them, were easier to treat as objects. Easier, but not easy. He had helped move two of them farther from the shelter so the living could stop smelling them. The work had been mechanical. His hands had known what to do even while his mind recited, over and over, that this was only temporary, that rescue was hours away, that no one would ever have to decide.

On the fifth morning the radio stayed silent and the sky stayed white. Someone—he never afterward remembered who—said the word aloud, very quietly, as if volume might make it real. No one answered. They sat with their backs to the metal and listened to their own stomachs.

He was the one who stood up. Not because he was braver. Because the shaking in his legs had become a kind of vote, and the vote was losing. He walked to the place they had left the dead and knelt. The cold had done part of the work already; the flesh was stiff, almost architectural. He told himself he was only looking. Then he told himself he was only testing whether the knife would even cut. The lie lasted until the blade met resistance and then gave.

What broke was not a single thought but the scaffolding that had held every thought in place. He had believed, without ever examining it, that there were acts a person simply could not perform and remain the same person. The belief had felt like a law of physics. When his hand brought the piece to his mouth, the law did not shatter so much as reveal itself to have been a story he had been told. The meat was frozen at the edges and tasted of nothing he could name—iron, and cold, and the particular sweetness of flesh that has begun to turn. His throat closed. He forced the swallow anyway, because the alternative was to spit it out and have to begin the argument with himself all over again.

Afterward he sat on his heels in the snow and waited to feel damned. What arrived instead was a thin, animal warmth low in his gut and a grief so large it had no edges. He understood, with a clarity that felt like another kind of hunger, that he would do it again tomorrow if tomorrow came. The person who could not have done it was already gone. He wiped his mouth with the back of his glove and walked back toward the living, carrying the knowledge like a second, heavier body.

The metal collar bit into his neck as the timer on the wall clicked down from sixty. The voice from the speaker was calm, almost bored. “Consume every last piece. The key is inside the last one. Or the collar detonates.”

The steel bowl sat on the table between his shackled wrists. Inside it, a glistening slab of raw liver the color of old brick, still warm, veins spidering across its surface. Maggots boiled over the edges in a pale, writhing carpet; cockroaches skittered beneath them, antennae twitching. The smell hit first—copper and ammonia and the sweet rot of meat left in the sun—thick enough to coat the back of his throat.

He gagged before he even touched it. Saliva flooded his mouth, hot and sour. His stomach clenched so hard his vision spotted. He forced his fingers into the mess. A cockroach crushed under his thumb with a wet pop; yellow guts smeared his skin. The liver was slick, heavy, and when he lifted a torn chunk the maggots rained off it onto his wrist, tiny hooks catching in the hair.

He shoved it in.

The texture was wrong in every way: cold slime giving way to fibrous chew, then the sudden frantic scramble of something still alive against his tongue. Bitter insect fluid burst across his taste buds—acrid, chemical, like battery acid mixed with shit. His throat locked. A violent heave rolled up from his gut; bile burned the back of his nose. He clamped his jaws and swallowed anyway, feeling the lump drag down, maggots still twitching as they went.

Another piece. Bigger. He had to bite through a vein; hot blood—his or the organ’s, he couldn’t tell—flooded his mouth and ran down his chin. The smell was inside him now. His eyes streamed. Every swallow triggered another spasm; his diaphragm bucked, trying to reverse the motion. Strings of spit and half-chewed gristle hung from his lips. A cockroach leg caught between his teeth and he retched so hard his vision went white, but nothing came up except a thin scream of air.

The timer hit twenty. He grabbed the last dripping handful, insects and all, and crammed it past his teeth. They crawled. He felt them on his soft palate, in the pockets of his cheeks. His gorge rose again—harder this time, a full-body convulsion that bowed his spine against the chains. He swallowed through it, throat clicking, tears and snot mixing with the blood on his face, until the bowl was empty and the only thing left moving was the frantic clench of his own stomach trying, and failing, to reject what he’d already forced down.

The priest’s hands did not tremble. In the black throat of the temple, where torchlight barely reached the altar’s grooves, he pressed the bound man’s shoulders flat against the stone with the same measured pressure he used to smooth a crease from his robe. The victim’s chest heaved; cords bit into wrists already raw. The priest noted the pulse under his palm the way a mason notes the grain of wood—present, irrelevant.

He selected the flint knife without looking at the man’s face. The first cut opened the abdomen just below the ribs, a clean lateral stroke that parted skin and the thin yellow layer of fat. Steam rose. The priest’s expression remained the slack, unlined mask it had worn since he entered the chamber; his eyes tracked the spill of blood only long enough to keep it from fouling the inscribed channels. Coils of intestine slid free, glistening, and he gathered them with both hands, lifting them clear so the next stroke could reach the diaphragm. A wet, rhythmic sound accompanied each breath the victim still managed. The priest did not blink at it.

When the heart was exposed he paused, not from reverence but to wipe the blade on the man’s own thigh so the edge would not slip. The final incision was short. He set the organ in the bronze bowl, arranged the remaining viscera according to the old pattern, and stepped back. His breathing had never changed. He wiped his hands on a square of linen, folded it once, and turned toward the next supplicant waiting in the dark, already calculating the angle of the first cut.

I tried to keep my eyes on the strip of sky. It seemed important. If I looked away, it might finish disappearing.

The cold crept inward from the fingers, patient, settling into the wrists, the elbows. When it reached my chest I understood it wasn’t the night. The night had been cold for hours. This was different. This was the heat leaving with the blood.

My heartbeat was the loudest thing left. It filled my ears, a wet, uneven thud that seemed to come from somewhere behind my eyes. Thump. A pause long enough to notice. Thump. Each one shoved a little more warmth out through the tear under my ribs. I could feel it sliding, slow and thick, soaking into the waistband of my shirt, pooling beneath me. The pavement drank it without comment.

I tried to count the beats. One. Two. The numbers slipped. Three became something else, a shape without edges. The light narrowed again. The fire escape was gone. Only a pale thread remained overhead, and even that trembled each time my heart struck.

Thump.

The cold reached my throat. Breathing turned into work. I pulled air in and it felt thin, already used. Somewhere far off a car passed, tires hissing on wet street, but the sound arrived muffled, as if through cloth. My own pulse was clearer. Closer. It stumbled—thump-thump, then a gap that stretched until I was sure it had stopped—then lurched back, weaker, apologetic.

The thread of sky frayed. I blinked and lost most of it. What remained was only brightness without color, and even that was leaking away at the corners the way the blood was leaking away beneath me. My heartbeat filled the dark it left behind. Slower now. Each strike a small, stubborn knock against the inside of my ribs, growing fainter, as if the thing making the sound were walking away down a long corridor.

Thump.

Cold all the way through. The light gone to a pinprick.

Thump.

I listened for the next one. The silence after it was wide and clean and did not end.

Thump.

The change began in the quiet hours, when Elias thought he was alone with the dark. At first it was only an itch beneath the skin of his forearms—an insistent, crawling wrongness, as if something coiled there had grown impatient. He scratched until the first layer split. Pale sheets of himself peeled away in damp, translucent ribbons, clinging to his nails before dropping to the floorboards with a soft, wet sound. Beneath lay new flesh, raw and too smooth, the color of bruised moonlight. It itched worse. He learned not to look at what he shed; the discarded skin kept the faint impression of his fingerprints, already fading.

The bones came next. He woke to the crack of his own ribs rearranging, each snap a bright, white shock that stole his breath and left him gasping on the mattress. His spine lengthened in stuttering increments; vertebrae ground and locked into a new curve that forced his shoulders forward and his head lower. Fingers thickened, joints reversing with audible pops until the hands no longer closed the way they once had. He bit down on a belt to keep from screaming and tasted copper. By morning the pain had dulled to a constant, grinding ache, and the new shape felt, horribly, more correct.

What frightened him most was how little he minded the rest. The neighbor’s dog had always barked at him; one night he simply stopped hearing it as noise and started hearing it as an invitation. When he found the animal later, throat opened in a single efficient motion, the warmth on his hands registered only as satisfaction. He stood over the body and waited for the old recoil—the guilt, the nausea, the frantic need to undo what he’d done. None of it arrived. In its place settled a cool, spacious clarity: the world was meat and distance, and he was no longer required to pretend otherwise.

He still wore Elias’s clothes for a while, though they split at the seams. He still answered to the name when someone called it from the street. But the voice that replied had changed register, lower and oddly patient, and the eyes that met theirs no longer flinched from what they saw. The last of the old skin sloughed away on a rain-slick night, leaving something that walked upright only when it chose to, and that no longer remembered why it had ever needed a reason to hurt.

PRISONER: You ever get used to this part?

EXECUTIONER: No.

PRISONER: Five minutes. They said five. Feels longer already.

EXECUTIONER: Sometimes it does.

PRISONER: You don't have to talk if you don't want. Most of them don't. They just stand there like furniture.

EXECUTIONER: I can talk.

PRISONER: Good. Silence makes it worse. Or maybe talking does. I don't know anymore.

(A pause.)

PRISONER: You got kids?

EXECUTIONER: One. A daughter.

PRISONER: How old?

EXECUTIONER: Nine.

PRISONER: She know what you do?

EXECUTIONER: She knows I work nights. That's enough for now.

PRISONER: Smart. Let her keep the other version of you a while longer.

EXECUTIONER: You have anyone coming?

PRISONER: No. My brother said he couldn't watch. I don't blame him. My mother died three years ago. Maybe that's a mercy.

(The prisoner looks at the clock, then away from it.)

PRISONER: You think I'm scared?

EXECUTIONER: I think anybody would be.

PRISONER: I am. Not of the dark, exactly. Of it being ordinary. Of everybody going home after and eating something. Of the world not even flinching.

EXECUTIONER: It flinches. Just not loud enough.

PRISONER: That's a kind thing to say. You practice that?

EXECUTIONER: No.

PRISONER: Then thank you.

(Another pause. Somewhere down the hall, a door closes.)

PRISONER: Can I ask you something real?

EXECUTIONER: Yes.

PRISONER: When it's over, do you go home and wash your hands like it matters? Or do you just sit in the car a while?

EXECUTIONER: I sit in the car.

PRISONER: How long?

EXECUTIONER: Until I can stand the sound of the engine.

PRISONER: Yeah. That sounds right.

(The prisoner breathes out, slow.)

PRISONER: I did what they say I did. I want that on the record, even if nobody's writing it down. I was angry and stupid and I took a life that wasn't mine to take. I've said sorry so many times it started sounding like a word I made up. It doesn't fix anything. I know that.

EXECUTIONER: I know you know.

PRISONER: Does it make this easier for you? That I admit it?

EXECUTIONER: No.

PRISONER: Good. I don't want it to be easy. Not for me. Not for you. If it gets easy, then something's wrong with both of us.

EXECUTIONER: Something's already wrong. That's why we're in this room.

PRISONER: Fair.

(The prisoner studies the executioner's face.)

PRISONER: You hate me?

EXECUTIONER: No.

PRISONER: Pity me?

EXECUTIONER: Some.

PRISONER: That's worse, isn't it?

EXECUTIONER: It's just true.

PRISONER: All right. I'll take true.

(A minute passes. Neither looks at the clock.)

PRISONER: If your daughter ever asks what kind of man you are, tell her you didn't look away. Tell her you stayed in the room. People remember the ones who stay.

EXECUTIONER: I'll tell her I tried to be decent when there wasn't a decent thing to do.

PRISONER: That'll do.

(Footsteps approach in the corridor. Both of them hear it.)

PRISONER: That's them.

EXECUTIONER: Yes.

PRISONER: One more thing.

EXECUTIONER: Go ahead.

PRISONER: After, when you're sitting in the car—don't pray for me if you don't mean it. But if you do mean it, say my name. Just once. So I'm not only the last thing that happened tonight.

EXECUTIONER: What's your name?

PRISONER: Daniel.

EXECUTIONER: All right, Daniel.

PRISONER: Thank you.

(The door opens. Light from the hall cuts across the floor.)

EXECUTIONER: I'll be there.

PRISONER: I know.

The darkness was absolute, pressing against his eyes like wet cloth. His shoulders jammed against wood on both sides; when he tried to lift a hand, his knuckles scraped the lid inches above his face. The air already tasted thin and hot, recycled through his own lungs.

A dull thud landed overhead. Then another. Dirt. He felt the vibration travel through the boards into his skull. He sucked in a breath that didn’t fill him and shoved upward with both palms. The lid didn’t budge. More thuds—faster now, a steady rain of soil—muffled and heavy. Each impact seemed to shrink the space by a fraction.

His chest hitched. He turned his head and his ear brushed the side wall; there was nowhere else to put it. The smell of raw earth seeped through the seams. He kicked, but his boots struck the foot of the box and the jolt rang through his bones without moving anything. Another load of dirt struck, closer, louder, sealing the last thin crack of sound from the world above. His next inhale caught halfway. The walls were still there, unmoving, and the air was gone.

The restraints bit into her wrists before the first incision. She was awake—sedation wasted resources—and the overhead lamps turned the operating theater into a white void where faces hovered like masks. A technician murmured calibration numbers. Then the saw began.

It was not the clean bite of steel she had imagined in nightmares. It was a wet, grinding vibration that traveled up the bone of her forearm and into her teeth. She screamed until her throat tore; the sound was swallowed by the machinery. They peeled muscle back in careful flaps, exposing the radius, and she felt every tug as if her nerves had been tuned to a higher frequency. Something cold and segmented was pressed into the cavity. It locked with a series of clicks that she heard inside her skull. When they cauterized the join, the smell of her own burning flesh filled her nose, sweet and metallic, and the pain flared white before settling into a deep, electric throb that would never fully leave.

Her left hand was gone. In its place, a lattice of carbon tendons and alloy joints flexed once, experimentally, under someone else’s command. She tried to make a fist and felt only the ghost of fingers that no longer existed, a phantom ache already being overwritten by new sensory feeds. Data scrolled across the inside of her eyelids—pulse, torque, remaining organic mass—while a voice she didn’t recognize counted down the percentage of her that still qualified as human.

They moved to the spine next. Each vertebrae they reinforced sent shocks down legs she could no longer command. She wept, not from the pain alone, but from the sudden, clinical understanding that the tears themselves were being logged as inefficient output. A port was seated at the base of her skull; when it seated, her memories flickered—childhood rooms, a lover’s mouth, the particular blue of a sky she would never see again—then recompiled into usable subroutines. She reached for her own name and found only a serial string.

By the time they wheeled her into the recovery bay, the screaming had stopped. What remained lay very still, chest rising in perfect mechanical rhythm, one eye already replaced by a lens that tracked the ceiling lights with inhuman patience. Somewhere beneath the new architecture, a small, wordless thing still understood what had been taken. It had no mouth left to say so.

The blood had dried in a perfect crescent along the marble floor, catching the late light like a stroke of vermilion on wet plaster. Elena crouched at the edge of the tape, gloved hands resting on her knees, and let the scene settle into her the way a painting settles when you stop trying to name it.

The victim lay on her side, one arm extended so the fingers just brushed the base of a toppled easel. The other arm was folded beneath her ribs, elbow bent at an angle that echoed the curve of the blood. Someone had arranged the hair—long, dark, still damp at the roots—so it fanned across the pale stone in a single deliberate sweep. No smears. No frantic arcs. Only the quiet geometry of a body that had been turned, once, and then left.

Elena’s camera hung unused against her chest. She already knew the measurements would confirm what her eye had measured: the distance from the crown of the head to the farthest fingertip matched, within a centimeter, the length of the shadow the easel threw across the wall. The killer had waited for the sun. She could see the faint tackiness where the blood had been guided, not splashed—thin lines drawn with something narrow, a brush or a gloved finger, connecting the pool beneath the torso to three smaller satellites near the feet. They formed a loose triangle whose apex pointed at the open window.

She rose slowly, careful not to disturb the air. From this height the composition clarified. The woman’s pale dress had been cut, not torn, along one seam so the fabric fell away from the shoulder in a single clean plane, exposing skin the color of unprimed canvas. A single pearl earring lay where it had been placed, not where it had fallen, exactly at the point where the jaw met the throat. Light from the window struck it and threw a tiny, hard highlight onto the floorboards beyond the marble—an accidental signature Elena knew she would not mention in the report.

Her partner called her name from the hallway. She didn’t answer at once. She was tracing, in her mind, the negative space: the empty rectangle of the missing canvas, the way the body’s curve completed a circle the room itself had only suggested. For a moment the yellow tape, the murmuring technicians, the distant siren all receded. There was only the arrangement, precise and unrepentant, and the low, private ache of recognition.

She lifted the camera at last. The shutter clicked once, twice. She would print the frames later, she decided, and keep the best one in the drawer she never showed anyone. Not as evidence. As study.

The first cut opened across his ribs without warning. One moment he was running, breath sawing, boots slamming wet earth; the next a line of fire unzipped his side and warm blood sheeted down into his waistband. He spun, arms up, and struck nothing. The air was empty. Only the sting remained, sharp and clean, as if a blade had kissed him and withdrawn before he could even flinch.

He staggered backward, pressing a hand to the wound. The skin was parted in a neat, shallow gash. No rustle of leaves. No footfall. Just the drip of his own blood onto the moss and the sudden, awful certainty that something stood close enough to touch him and he could not see it.

A pressure bloomed against his shoulder—solid, heavy, almost curious—then vanished. He lashed out with his knife and the blade met only cold air. His pulse hammered so hard his vision pulsed with it. Every hair on his arms lifted. The forest smells sharpened: wet bark, his own sweat, the copper already rising from the cut. He turned in a slow circle, knife extended, and felt the skin between his shoulder blades prickle as if eyes were fixed there. Or not eyes. Something that did not need them.

Pain exploded across the back of his calf. He went down hard, knee striking a root, and the unseen edge dragged upward, parting denim and flesh in one continuous stroke. He screamed and rolled, swinging wildly. His knuckles cracked against a tree. Nothing else. The wound burned and throbbed in time with his heart, blood soaking his sock, and still he could not find the thing that had done it. It was not hiding. It was simply not there to be seen, and that absence felt worse than any shape.

He dragged himself upright, weight on the good leg, and the air in front of his face stirred—warm, damp, smelling faintly of old meat and rain. He froze. Something exhaled against his cheek. The breath was slow, deliberate. He could feel the heat of it, the faint moisture, and then a fingertip—or what might have been a fingertip—traced the line of his jaw with terrible gentleness before hooking, sudden and deep, into the soft place beneath his ear.

He tore free, skin ripping, and ran. Behind him there was no pursuit he could hear. Only the wet sound of his own blood hitting the leaves, and the knowledge, colder than the night, that the next touch could come from anywhere, at any moment, and he would never see it coming.
